item.title: Pretend Empathy Is Now a Product
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Pretend Empathy Is Now a Product

AI therapy offers connection without the cost of being known by another human.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • AI therapy provides a kind of "pretend empathy." Millions of people find it genuinely helpful.
  • The most clinically rigorous AI therapy chatbot shut down in 2025. The unregulated ones are thriving.
  • Healing requires friction: mutual vulnerability, the risk of being misunderstood, and sustained presence.
  • A chatbot will never misunderstand you or ask for anything. That frictionlessness is the problem.
Source: Sanket Mishra/Pexels

Psychiatry once promised to heal the soul. Then came the 15-minute appointment, the prescription pad, and eventually the AI chatbot—and the soul became a friction the system could not afford.

I spent some time in a state forensic psychiatric hospital, and I have some thoughts.

Sherry Turkle, the MIT psychologist who studies our relationship with technology, calls what AI therapy platforms offer "pretend empathy." They anticipate appropriate responses, reflect your anguish back to you, offering a simulacrum of being heard. Turkle warns that technology seduces us with "the illusion of companionship without the demands of friendship." A chatbot will never misunderstand you, express impatience, or need anything in return. That frictionlessness is the selling point.

And it works, to a point. Clinical trials show real reductions in symptoms of depression and anxiety, but only over two weeks, and only in mild to moderate cases. Many people who would never dare to set foot in a therapist's office will open an app at 3 a.m. and may temporarily feel relief. They may feel as if someone is finally listening. Any honest argument about AI therapy has to start there.

Venture capital has seized on the opportunity. Investment in digital mental health has skyrocketed to more than $2 billion a year. The FDA has conferred Breakthrough Device designations to some digital therapeutics, including Woebot's CBT-based program for postpartum depression. Britain's National Health Service has experimented with routing patients on therapy waiting lists to AI chatbots until they can meet face-to-face with a clinician. The pitch is enticing precisely because the problem is real: one in five American adults lives with a mental illness, half will never get treatment, and psychiatry is confronting the most dire workforce shortage of any medical specialty.

More alarming, the rigorous version failed. In June 2025, Woebot Health, among the most thoroughly studied AI therapy platforms ever built, backed by Stanford researchers, with $124 million in venture capital and a Breakthrough Device designation, closed its consumer app. Woebot was built on clinical evidence and structured therapeutic scripts; however, consumer churn was too high, the regulatory path too slow, and free large-language-model chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude were proliferating with no clinical scripting and no regulatory oversight. The most responsible product in the category could not survive. The least accountable ones are thriving.

article continues after advertisement

This is the pattern in psychiatry. A hospital administrator once observed that people used to want to be psychiatrists because they wanted to talk to their patients, but managed care ended that. The 15-minute appointment became the clinical norm. Psychiatrists now specialize in pharmacological calibration, trained to match the right diagnosis to the right molecule. The prescription pad replaced the couch. And now AI therapy has arrived in the robotic vacancy that managed care left behind, offering the latest version of the same bargain: care without the friction of human encounter.

Now comes the uncomfortable part. A chatbot often offers more psychological attention than the existing human system. Imagine a patient whose chatbot says, You mentioned three days ago that you were afraid your brother was going to leave. Is that still weighing on you? Now imagine the same patient's 15-minute med check: Any suicidal ideation? Thoughts of harming others? How are you sleeping? Appetite okay? Here's your refill and I'll see you in six months. We can expect that people will form attachments to machines when institutions have made human attention this scarce.

That paradox indicts our culture more than the technology. The philosopher Jonathan Lear once asked whether we want more from psychiatry than to get a person back to work "in the cheapest, most efficient way." We answered that question decades ago when we defunded the talking cure. AI therapy is inheriting the consequences.

But Turkle's deeper point: What do we lose as human beings when we accept the frictionless substitute? The danger is that "pretend empathy" feels like empathy. It may even function like empathy. What it cannot do is what healing actually requires: it cannot challenge you, cannot sit with you in a silence that grows uncomfortable, cannot risk the relationship by telling you something you do not want to hear. The psychiatrists Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini, and Richard Lannon have a name for what that encounter engages: limbic resonance, the mutual neural attunement through which two mammals regulate each other's emotional states. As I wrote in a recent post, this is what it felt like when my therapist Susan finally saw me after 14 months of institutionalization. Psychotherapy implicates physiology. A chatbot can mimic language. It cannot enter into limbic resonance with you because it has no limbic brain.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

Charlie, a patient on my unit at Mendota, had spent years revolving between maximum and medium security (not his real name). He had been given medication after medication, told to try harder to control his voices. Near the end of my stay, he transferred to a new team. Their first meeting lasted 45 minutes. Not only did they listen, but they stayed with him to ask about his life before the hospital, about his family, about the contours of the voices that kept him up at night. Those voices, after playing years of pharmaceutical roulette, began to quiet. That encounter had everything a chatbot cannot give: investment, friction, attention to the past and the possibility of the future, and the honest vulnerability of one person's presence with another.

To be clear, AI will reach some people, and some of them will find genuine relief, at least for a time. We should honor that. And we should also be honest about what the frictionless age is asking us to accept: that a performance of empathy so approximates the real thing that we stop asking for it from our institutions, our clinicians, and ourselves. The more we seek companionship in machines, the less we practice the harder, slower, riskier work of knowing and being known by another human being. Turkle fears that we will forget what we are missing. After all, the talking cure was lost to a culture that chose efficiency over intimacy—and pretend empathy is just the latest manifestation of that preference.

item.title: Why Cannabis Hyperemesis Is Sending More People to the ER
item.description:
Cannabis

Why Cannabis Hyperemesis Is Sending More People to the ER

New CDC data reveal a condition that may be underrecognized.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • The CDC found nearly 200,000 emergency visits involving cannabis hyperemesis from 2023 to 2026.
  • Reported rates rose sharply after CHS received its own diagnostic code in October 2025.
  • People aged 15 to 24 had the highest rate of CHS-related emergency visits.
Source: Budding / Unsplash

A new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is drawing attention to cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), a condition associated with frequent cannabis use that causes recurrent episodes of severe nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

From January 2023 through May 2026, the CDC identified 199,565 emergency department visits involving CHS, with the proportion of these visits increasing substantially after a new diagnostic code for the syndrome was introduced in October 2025.

The timing is important because the new figures do not necessarily mean that CHS suddenly became much more common. Before October 2025, there was no specific diagnostic code for the condition, so doctors had to identify possible cases using combinations of codes for vomiting and cannabis-related diagnoses. Once CHS received its own code, it became much easier to recognize and record.

The CDC therefore believes that at least part of the increase reflects better detection of a condition that had probably been underestimated.

That distinction does not make the findings less relevant. The higher numbers give healthcare professionals a better indication of how often CHS is reaching emergency departments and highlight a condition that can remain unrecognized even in people who have been treated for repeated episodes of vomiting.

What is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome?

Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome is characterized by repeated episodes of intense nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain in people who use cannabis frequently. The episodes can be severe enough to cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances and require emergency medical care. Symptoms may disappear for a period of time and then return, particularly when cannabis use continues.

The condition can be particularly confusing, since cannabis is also used in medicine to treat certain types of nausea and vomiting. A person who uses cannabis for another health problem may therefore have little reason to suspect that it could be contributing to their gastrointestinal symptoms.

CHS is generally associated with heavy, frequent, and prolonged cannabis use, although the CDC notes that symptoms may begin sooner than previously thought. Some evidence suggests that they can appear within the first year of use, rather than only after many years of regular consumption.

article continues after advertisement

Why is CHS often missed?

There is no single test that confirms cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. Doctors have to consider the patient's symptoms and cannabis use while also looking for other possible causes of recurrent vomiting.

That can be difficult in practice because patients do not always mention cannabis use, and clinicians may not routinely ask about it. CHS can also resemble cyclic vomiting syndrome and other gastrointestinal conditions, so a person may be treated for vomiting without the connection to cannabis being recognized.

One of the more distinctive clues is a strong tendency to take very hot showers or baths because the heat temporarily relieves nausea or abdominal discomfort. This behavior is associated with CHS, but it is not enough by itself to establish the diagnosis.

What do the CDC numbers show?

Before the new diagnostic code was introduced, CHS was identified in about 3.2 emergency department visits per 10,000 visits on average. After the code became available, that figure rose to about 12 per 10,000, nearly four times as high. In May 2026, it reached 13.1 per 10,000.

The abrupt change is one reason the CDC does not interpret it as evidence that the actual incidence of CHS suddenly quadrupled. The researchers point instead to improved recognition and documentation, although the higher numbers may provide a more accurate picture of the syndrome's impact on emergency care.

The data also show that CHS-related visits were particularly common among younger people. From October 2025 through May 2026, the proportion among people aged 15 to 24 was 38.7 per 10,000 emergency department visits, compared with 28.3 among those aged 25 to 34 and 3.5 among people aged 45 and older.

Could stronger cannabis products be contributing?

Cannabis products have become more potent over time, while vaping, concentrates, and other forms of consumption have become increasingly common. This matters because frequent cannabis use is the main risk factor associated with CHS, and higher-potency products have been linked to more frequent cannabis use among adolescents and young adults.

article continues after advertisement

However, the CDC does not conclude that higher THC concentration directly causes CHS. The relationship is more complicated and more research is needed to determine whether potency itself changes the risk of developing the syndrome.

The same uncertainty applies to newer products and consumption methods. The CDC says further surveillance is needed to determine whether product type, potency, route of administration, and changing patterns of use are influencing CHS.

How is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome treated?

Treatment during an acute episode focuses on controlling vomiting and addressing dehydration or electrolyte abnormalities when they occur. Severe cases may require intravenous fluids and other emergency care.

Preventing another episode requires a different approach. Stopping cannabis use is the treatment that addresses the underlying cause of CHS, and symptoms generally resolve after cannabis is discontinued. Continuing to use cannabis can allow the episodes to return.

This can be particularly complicated for people who use cannabis to manage chronic pain, sleep problems, anxiety, or another health condition. In those cases, stopping cannabis may require finding another way to manage the original symptoms rather than simply removing the substance from the treatment plan.

What should cannabis users know?

The new CDC data make CHS easier to see, but they also raise a broader question about how often recurrent vomiting is being attributed to other causes when cannabis use is not considered. The new diagnostic code gives clinicians a more specific way to identify the syndrome and will also make it easier to track its prevalence over time.

For patients, the most useful takeaway is that cannabis use is relevant medical information regardless of why it is being used. As more cases are identified consistently, future data should provide a clearer picture of who develops CHS and whether changes in cannabis products and patterns of use are affecting its occurrence.

item.title: 5 Steps to Finding Meaning and Purpose
item.description:
Positive Psychology

5 Steps to Finding Meaning and Purpose

Suggestions for helping access the most important parts of human existence.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning and purpose are difficult to find, but, like many things, their difficulty makes them important.
  • Finding meaning is best treated as a process and not a single step you have to get right the first time.
  • Treat each activity and experience in your life as a way of helping you get further to defining meaning.
  • Even experiences that end up not feeling meaningful give you insight as to how you define purpose.

Social evolution has led human beings to look for ways to make what they do every day feel important beyond just survival. For centuries, human beings were focused only on getting through every day, so meaning and purpose in their lives were primarily focused on finding shelter and food. That pretty much took up every day.

Notice I talk here about “social evolution.” From a psychological point of view, social evolution is much more important than genetic evolution. Genetic evolution is important and primarily focuses on the physiological factors that contribute to how we respond to our environment. But social evolution, from an emotional and behavioral standpoint, is even more important because it offers much explanation for how we respond to our physiological reactions and our environment.

Searching for meaning and purpose beyond just survival and reproduction is much more the result of social evolution than of genetic evolution.

Not only are meaning and purpose beyond survival important for humans. They are very much what makes us human beings and different from non-human beings.

With that in mind, here is a summary of five major steps that are very important for helping to find meaning and purpose in life:

1. Work not only on identifying goals but on identifying what you generally value in life

Look at what you already find meaningful and ask yourself, “What does this tell me about what I truly value?" This could be valuing relationships, valuing contributions to society, or valuing commitment to a specific religious faith. All of those can be important for meaning, provided they are what you think is important and not what other people tell you should be important.

2. Commit yourself to engaging in meaningful activities instead of waiting for those activities to appear

Finding meaning and purpose often develops through continued involvement in important things like work, relationships, caregiving, creativity, and community activities. But people often have to look for those activities rather than waiting for them to occur. Searching for purpose is very much an active process, and sometimes you have to try different things to see if they are meaningful. Even if you try them and determine they’re not meaningful, at least you have made an attempt.

3. Actively look for ways to contribute something beyond yourself

Even if you engage in a community or caregiving activity and do not immediately find it meaningful, it can be useful to ask yourself whether it seems other people found it beneficial. Sometimes determining meaning does not come from your initial internal response but comes from how other people respond to what you are doing. If they find what you are doing meaningful, then it might become more meaningful to you. But notice this does not mean that you base meaning on what people tell you is meaningful, but rather on what you experience from how people respond to you.

article continues after advertisement

4. Use your experiences to develop a coherent understanding of meaning and purpose

As you have experiences you find meaningful or not, each one helps you figure out what you find meaningful overall. Reflect on each experience that you have and look at it in the context of other experiences to try to develop a coherent personal philosophy of meaning and purpose.

5. Treat meaning and purpose as things that can change through time and experiences and not something you have to get absolutely right the first time

Finding meaning and purpose is very much a process and will often involve modification to what you think is meaningful and purposeful. Do not be afraid to allow experiences to show you that maybe something you thought was meaningful and purposeful before is not as meaningful and purposeful as you thought it was.

Finding meaning and purpose is very important not only for a life that feels complete but also for psychological health. Treating it as an active process where each experience is allowed to add to your view can be a very helpful way to access meaning and purpose.

item.title: Are You Calling Your College Freshman Too Much?
item.description:
Parenting

Are You Calling Your College Freshman Too Much?

Redefining support for young adults at college.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Young adulthood requires a shift in the relationship dynamic between parents and their kids.
  • Keeping conversations relatively short helps make them more inviting for kids, who fear getting “trapped.”
  • Avoid asking your college kid too many things about school and instead express an interest in them.

Do I text her too much? The answer: Probably. If you’re asking this, you have likely gone a little overboard.

No shame in that, though. You lived with your child 24/7, and now, in some cases, it is utter radio silence, a situation of not knowing. You have to wonder how much of that radio silence means: too busy with schoolwork, as she says? And how much is her way of taking some space or setting a new boundary? There is also the question of what boundaries are appropriate for your kid to set, and which are expressions of overconfidence or intentional exclusion?

How often to call or text becomes especially tricky if you’re aware your child is feeling overwhelmed or anxious or homesick or depressed. You might ask your son or daughter how much checking in is okay. You can say, Hey, I know this has been a challenging first semester and that you’re not very happy right now. It makes me want to check in with you a lot more than I have been, but I don’t want to be annoying. What feels supportive to you, and what feels like too much?

People say the early years of raising children are the hardest, but big challenges come at all ages, even into adulthood. Young adults may not need their parents to be as involved as they had been, but it doesn’t mean they wouldn’t welcome it when available and in their service, not the parents’.

Keep the conversation flowing when living apart for the first time.

Keep the calls short

Many people avoid talking on the phone with certain people because they can’t get off the call. Shorter calls, 10 or 15 minutes, are much more welcome by college students. They can focus on what you are saying instead of planning an exit strategy.

Don’t make the call all about school

Nothing is less appealing to a college student than a conversation with their parents in which they’re asked the same questions they were asked in middle and high school: Do you have any homework? Are you ready for your Spanish test? Did you get everything you need to finish that history project you told me about? Unless there are notable academic problems, make the conversation about other topics: What has surprised her most about college life? What aspects of college life have been disappointing? How do kids generally find their friend groups on campus? Is being on her own more fun or freeing or anxiety-provoking than she thought it would be? Questions like these show interest in your kid’s experience of being away from home for the first time, and not just on their performance.

Make sure it’s a conversation, not an interview

Many exchanges between parents and their college-aged sons and daughters contain questions from the parents and answers from the kids. Over and over again. Pretty boring. Exchanges in which one person only is asked to show up (in this case, the kid) rarely get off the ground. Parents need to show up, too. That means becoming part of the exchange, sharing what’s interesting about you and your life, so that it becomes a conversation rather than a quick check-in.

article continues after advertisement

To stack the deck in favor of a terrific, sustaining parent-adult child relationship is talking with your kid with the same respect and courtesy you would extend to anyone else whose connection you value. In some families with kids entering young adulthood, the communications continue along the same lines of the “business” of parenting (make sure you__, don’t forget to__) or with a familiar banter that can be funny in the moment but lacks the authenticity of real conversations in which people get to know one another.

It’s never too late to say, I want something more out of our conversations, love, but I don’t even know what that looks like. I know that I’ve spent the last 18 years making sure you were okay and had everything you needed, but you don’t need that from me anymore. It’s weird. If we’re not figuring out how you can do your travel team while still doing the musical, or if we’re not arguing, I don’t even know what we’d talk about! It’s sad, and I’d really like to change that. What do you think?

Your kid might look at you as if to say, Who are you? But your candor and genuine invitation to join you in a more meaningful way could spark a curiosity that opens doors to conversations and a depth of relationship you didn’t know existed.

item.title: What to Do When Narcissists Rain on Your Parade
item.description:
Narcissism

What to Do When Narcissists Rain on Your Parade

Are you strong enough to raise your umbrella against the narcissism storm?

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissistic parents can be jealous of their own children.
  • You don't need anyone’s permission to be happy.
  • Protecting your own happiness isn’t selfish.
Source: Ohlamor Studio / Unsplash

Have you ever noticed how some people seem to have a gift for raining on your parade? If you have a narcissist in your life at home, at work, as a friend, or in your family, you have had the unfortunate experience of them being unable to celebrate your happiness or joy. It’s like they often dim the light and bring up something negative, so it literally feels like they just ruined it. It may be your happy mood, an accomplishment, a dream, an idea, or just moments when you are truly shining and proud of it.

Narcissistic parents seem to be unusually good at this gift. Why? Don’t most parents want their children to be happy and successful? Well, unfortunately, no. But we can recognize the behavior, see it as their problem or their internal chaos, and choose not to engage in it. They create the storm, but we don’t have to stand in it. We are not responsible for other people’s reactions. When someone rains on our parade, we are only responsible for how we deal with it for our own mental health and happiness.

Why Do People Rain?

People raining on your parade has everything to do with them and their own sense of self. Narcissistic parents typically want you to do well enough that you reflect well on them, but not so well that you outshine them, because then they become jealous of you. But why? Here are some possible explanations.

  • They are unhappy and insecure themselves, and it makes them feel worse if someone else is happy.
  • Their own feelings about their life are dismal, and they don’t feel good about who they are.
  • They may have a lack of empathy or not know how to tune in emotionally to you.
  • They may think they are protecting you from all the negatives that could happen.
  • They may just want to control you. They don’t want you to change. Change rattles people.
  • Maybe they haven't received support and validation in their lives, and they don’t know how to give it.
  • They are just plain jealous of you.

When They Rain on Your Parade, Raise the Umbrella!

Your response to the rain is directly related to how you feel about yourself. It’s important to believe in yourself, and to give yourself permission to enjoy the good things that you have created in your life. It’s inevitable that some people, maybe even your own parents or family members, don’t really understand you. That’s okay if you get you. We can learn to get out of the rain and protect our joy.

article continues after advertisement

If you are dealing with narcissists, lower your expectations of what they can give you. The wishing and hoping they will change is exhausting and not worth it.

Look for people who do understand you and can celebrate who you are. They are out there. Don’t let the negativity of others control your movement in life or how you feel about yourself. Someone wanting you to feel small so they can feel big is simply not okay. When we see it, we can block it with our boundaries and self-validation. (Raise that umbrella!) Our playing small so that others can feel better does not serve anyone.

My client, Laura, at age 33, was constantly nagged by her mother about her weight. She was put on diets at a very early age, and her appearance was everything to her mother. But when Laura was in her 20s, she got a great trainer and lost weight at the same time her mother gained weight. Laura’s mother could not handle the fact that Laura looked better than she did. Laura shared the following with me:

“After my weight loss and fitness work, whenever I’d see Mom, she would call me anorexic. I’ve never had an eating disorder of any kind, but she would say things like ‘get your anorexic, skinny butt over here and do the dishes for me.’ It was so hurtful. Why couldn’t she just be proud of me? Thankfully, I am doing my continued recovery work and can see that my mom is just jealous. I think it is sad for her, but I get to be me, and that includes being the best me I can be.”

Elbert Hubbard, writer and philosopher, wraps it up like this: “To avoid criticism, say nothing, do nothing, be nothing.”

item.title: What Palliative Care Teaches Us About Living Well
item.description:
Caregiving

What Palliative Care Teaches Us About Living Well

Giving back patients control of their own care journey.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Palliative care isn't the end of treatment, it runs alongside curative care while easing pain and anxiety.
  • Feeling understood is protective: Patients who feel understood carry less anxiety and depression.
  • Serious illness burdens families too; good palliative care extends real support to unprepared caregivers.
  • Access to home palliative care still depends on insurance and geography, a solvable problem in medicine today.

When I reflect on my 20 years of practicing palliative medicine, the biggest takeaway is how the setting changes the work. Sitting down at a kitchen table with a patient and their family, instead of standing at a hospital bedside or in a clinic, changes the relationship. The person in front of me is in the comfort of their own home, surrounded by the people and objects that hold their history, and the conversation becomes theirs to lead.

Much of the public still misunderstands what palliative care is. They assume that opting into it means that their treatment is ending, or that a clinical team has decided there is nothing more to offer. That couldn’t be further from the truth.

Palliative care is for anyone living with serious illness. People can receive it while continuing treatment for various serious illnesses, such as cancer, cardiac disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, kidney and liver failure, or neurological conditions. A palliative care team, which includes physicians, nurses, social workers, and chaplains, supports a patient’s medical care—helping with symptoms, difficult decisions, communication, and importantly, making sure the patient has a voice in what happens next.

When someone is seriously ill, their families often make important choices for them. Suddenly, a person who has always made their own decisions may feel as though they are being carried along by the medical system. Our job in palliative care is to slow that down and help them live the life they want. For me, providing palliative care is the most fulfilling part of the job.

I recall a time I worked with a patient who had lung cancer that was progressing quickly. My colleague, a social worker, and I had a meeting with the patient and his daughters, who assumed his best option was to continue aggressive treatment at the hospital. When asked what he wanted to do, he told us he wanted to play golf, and he was upset that he never would again.

I remember saying, “Why can't you play golf?” He said, “Well, look at me.” I replied, “Okay, but you live with grass right around your house. Why don’t we set up a putting green for you? You'll stand up. You'll putt. You'll play golf.”

Everyone's mood in the room changed. Although the patient passed away shortly after our time with him, he spent those last weeks the way he wanted to live. Bringing the opportunity to feel joy back into the lives of these patients is so rewarding. It inspires me to live well myself.

In my experience, the sickest patients want to be home. Living at home means being surrounded by the memories and objects that make up who they are. Many families are hesitant to take a loved one home because they don’t want to take on the risk or don’t have the resources to take on the risk.

One of my patients, the matriarch of her family, loved to paint rocks. I would visit her monthly as her health declined, and she gifted me a painted rock with a bunny on it that I still have on my desk. Another one of my patients willed me her art of Chagall windows, which I now have hanging in my own home. It is special when a patient feels close enough to you to share something sentimental to them, and it reflects a level of intimacy in care that is difficult to achieve outside of the home.

article continues after advertisement

Palliative care is often mental. I never use those words “this is the end” with my patients. We are always very much in the moment. Instead, I ask questions like, “What can we do to make this better?” and “What can we do to improve your situation?” Alongside symptom management, home-based palliative care allows the care team to be present with patients.

It takes a full team. Physicians or nurse practitioners take the lead on medicine. Registered nurses quarterback symptom management and conduct goals of care conversations. Social workers navigate family dynamics and handle social determinants of health like food insecurity. Lastly, chaplains help patients process the spiritual and existential questions that serious illness raises.

Palliative care, delivered well and delivered at home, is about helping people live as fully as they can for as long as they have, with a team of advocates who listen closely and center the care around the patient’s values. For patients, it offers a new opportunity to stay engaged with life. As a practitioner, it reminds me of the value of choice and the small moments that make life worth living. Being allowed into that space, again and again, remains a privilege.

item.title: The Shadow Artificial Third: AI Use in Therapy
item.description:
Therapeutic Alliance

The Shadow Artificial Third: AI Use in Therapy

How AI-drafted responses may impact the therapeutic relationship.

Posted September 2, 2026

Source: Unseen Studio / Unsplash

“What is originality, after all, but the shape that results from the natural impulse to communicate to others that feeling of freedom, that unconstrained joy?”
― Haruki Murakami, Novelist as a Vocation

"I would be very upset if I found out my therapist was using AI to write emails to me," I heard recently.

I understood this intuitively. AI-generated drafting and writing is fast becoming ubiquitous. I recently started to write back to a friend and saw there was an entire email drafted in the window—in wording I would never use. There appears to be no way to avoid the presence of AI-assisted language. LinkedIn has been found to be the most saturated platform, with an estimated 41% of long-form text that appears there being AI-generated.

Generative AI drafting tools are now frequently built into electronic medical record systems to assist clinicians. Yet people still seem to prefer human-generated messages—even though, as one study found, AI-generated messages may be rated more empathic. But AI-generated empathy may be template-driven, while human-generated responses are more diverse, according to another recent study.

The Shadow Artificial Third

This hypothetical case of the clinician using generative AI to draft emails falls under the specter of the artificial third in the therapeutic relationship, a term from Yuval Haber et al. describing "a new artificial presence" in therapy. Here, it is quietly brought in by the clinician—a shadow AI use I describe as the shadow artificial third.

Shadow artificial third can refer to secret AI use by either clinicians -- or clients who may be using large language models (LLMs) for emotional support, companionship, or personal guidance in ways that they do not share with their therapist or clinicians.

Therapists may turn to generative AI tools to draft communications for understandably different reasons—wishing to integrate helpful informational resources, craft more empathic statements, or save time, or perhaps the feature is just integrated within the platform they use.

A recent study published in the New England Journal of Medicine AI found that an electronic health record-integrated AI email drafting feature may not provide as much time savings as one might think. A 2025 study found that AI-drafting tools were used by less than 20% of healthcare professionals and reduced time spent on patient communication by about 7%. It is unclear if this will improve as clinicians become more facile with reviewing AI-generated drafts and as systems improve.

But the deeper concern is that words are our way of connecting and seeing each other and so bringing an artificial third into that relationship—and then concealing it—can feel like a betrayal. Language is often our way of sharing who we are, in our own voice, and conveying a sense of care. What happens when that care becomes AI-assisted? To use AI in communications in a therapeutic relationship, especially if it involves content beyond scheduling logistics, can feel akin to a Cyrano de Bergerac-like betrayal.

article continues after advertisement

Transparency and Other Ethical Issues

This hypothetical situation also raises several ethical questions, such as whether clinicians should disclose generative AI use in patient/client communications or other clinical situations. Transparency of AI use in these situations seems essential, as it can help the receiver calibrate their trust in the information contained within a message. I believe this applies even when it involves tools integrated into the electronic health record systems. For example, it seems more important to note this in communications that may contain informational resources versus basic scheduling logistics.

But it raises a deeper question: whether AI-generated drafts should be used in the first place in communications, particularly in situations involving a relationship based on psychotherapy.

Using AI in communications in a psychotherapy relationship involves special considerations. It is similar to issues involved in adopting ambient AI scribes, which has different privacy and therapeutic alliance considerations related to psychotherapy, such as privacy and confidentiality, data security, the impact on the therapeutic alliance, and whether its presence might have a chilling effect on the disclosure of sensitive information.

AI-assisted writing tools can help other medical specialties like surgery, but those relationships and subject matter are different.

The inherent "jagged" nature of this technology means that there may be more effective use cases than others. AI-assisted writing is likely useful in many clinical situations. It may also depend on the clinician's baseline level of comfort and skill with writing, communication type, and the intended purpose (e.g., to offer useful clinical information versus conveying empathy).

Diminishing Diversity of the Linguistic Landscape

A final consideration: AI-assisted writing is resulting in less diversity in the linguistic landscape. This was recently demonstrated in a study across multiple domains and 880,000 texts, finding that LLMs are homogenizing our writing. This raises the question, even if AI-drafted communications become more efficient over time, what is the cost of this efficiency? What do we lose along with the diversity of our communications: our identities, voice, authenticity, emotional expressiveness, or our investment of care?

article continues after advertisement

As Haruki Murakami wrote, “One opposite of imagination is 'efficiency.'”

For some, writing is an expression of identity, of the self. I often spend many hours helping clients who have focused so much on efficiency that they have lost touch with other priorities-- their self-expression, freedom, joy, and investing time on things that have friction and take time and effort, like human connection. It is almost as if an efficiency addiction develops, a compulsion toward frictionless experiences, that makes it hard to enjoy the diversity and surprises of the human experience.

Of course, I am not opposed to AI use when well-placed and mutually beneficial to client and clinician, but there may be something worthwhile in putting our effort into something-- even if the outcome is less perfect-- especially when it can capture who we are. There is a gift in discovering ourselves through writing-- and in sharing that with each other.

item.title: A Climate Future You Can Step Into
item.description:
Environment

A Climate Future You Can Step Into

Using time travel in VR to study how people respond to environmental change.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Virtual reality can make different possible futures feel personal.
  • Using VR, participants can travel across generations.
  • Climate damage can become a lived experience with VR.
  • In an experiment, carbon footprints fell after the VR experience, and some effects remained six weeks later.

You begin as a child. Through the windows of a virtual home, animals graze in a green field. A parent sits nearby while the television reports on climate change. Then time advances. You are older, and so is your parent. The room has deteriorated. Beyond the glass, fires burn in the distance.

Time jumps again. Now you are the parent. A child turns to you and pleads for their future. The television is dead. Outside, the landscape has been emptied.

Then comes one final journey, 50 years ahead. This future is different. In a virtual museum, you learn that mass public pressure forced political leaders to act. The worst outcome was not inevitable after all.

This is an experiment designed to investigate a difficult question: Can people’s environmental attitudes change when the future is no longer something they merely hear about, but somewhere they feel they have lived?

Turning distance into experience

Climate change presents psychologists with an unusual problem. Its causes stretch across countries, industries, and generations. Many of its most severe consequences lie beyond the horizon of everyday life. A graph can show rising temperatures, but it cannot easily convey what it might feel like to age inside a changing climate, or to explain that change to a child who must live with it.

Virtual reality offers researchers a way to manipulate this psychological distance. It can place people inside environments that do not yet exist, while carefully controlling what they see and how they encounter it.

In the study, conducted by Yuke Pi and colleagues, 41 participants experienced the same four-part journey through past, present, and possible futures. Twenty-one entered it through a life-sized avatar whose movements followed their own. They could look down and see a body, watch it move in a mirror, and interact with objects in the room. The remaining 20 watched the same events as invisible observers, without a virtual body. The researchers called the first experience embodiment: in everyday language, this means that the virtual body can begin to feel temporarily like your body. You know intellectually that the hands and reflection are computer-generated, yet your perceptual system treats them as belonging to you.

That distinction allowed the researchers to ask something more precise than whether VR is persuasive. Both groups saw the same damaged home, burning landscape, and hopeful conclusion. What differed was whether participants watched a family endure climate change or occupied a place within that family.

Environmental attitudes are more than concern

It is relatively easy to ask whether someone is worried about climate change. But worry alone may not lead anywhere, as a person can be deeply concerned while also believing that individual action is futile.

The researchers therefore measured several different responses: participants rated whether they believed their own actions could influence climate change and whether acting might encourage other people to join them. They also reported intentions to sign petitions, contact public officials, attend demonstrations, and take part in other forms of collective action.

article continues after advertisement

The researchers also used a carbon footprint calculator covering food, travel, household energy, and consumption. Participants completed it before the VR session, two weeks later, and again after six weeks. This moved the study beyond a single questionnaire administered while the experience was still fresh.

The results were promising, but not simple.

Participants in both groups reported lower estimated carbon footprints after the experience, including at the six-week follow-up. The early reduction appeared larger among those who had occupied a virtual body. Immediately after the session, participants also expressed a stronger sense that their actions mattered and could encourage others. Political participation intentions rose sharply, while reports collected six weeks later suggested that some increase in climate-related activity remained.

Embodiment seemed to intensify some short-term reactions, but it was not consistently superior. The story itself, including its movement through time, its family relationships, its catastrophic scenes, and its hopeful ending, may have done much of the work.

A collective route to hope

The experiment did not end amid flames and abandonment. That decision is scientifically important.

A frightening future can create urgency, but it can also produce helplessness. If disaster appears complete and unavoidable, there is little reason to act. The final scene offered what psychologists sometimes call constructive hope: hope based not on denying the danger, but on showing a believable route through it.

article continues after advertisement

In this case, that route was collective pressure. The future improved because citizens protested, spread information, and pushed institutions to respond. The scenario therefore connected individual influence with coordinated political action instead of implying that climate change could be solved through private consumer choices alone.

Yet the study cannot tell us which ingredient was decisive. Participants encountered disaster, aging, parenthood, real news footage, interactive objects, and an optimistic resolution in a single sequence. Future experiments could separate these elements: catastrophe with and without hope, embodiment with and without aging, or private lifestyle messages compared with collective-action messages.

A laboratory for possible worlds

The findings reveal what VR can contribute to environmental research.

Its real value is not simply that it makes climate change look dramatic. Film can do that. VR allows researchers to alter the participant’s position inside the drama. They can hold a future constant while changing whether someone watches it, inhabits it, causes it, survives it, or remembers it.

That makes virtual reality less like a crystal ball and more like a wind tunnel for environmental psychology. It cannot predict exactly how society will respond to climate change. But it can create controlled possible worlds and test which experiences make people return to the real one prepared to behave differently.

item.title: How Students Are Learning to Consider and Update Beliefs
item.description:
Education

How Students Are Learning to Consider and Update Beliefs

Joanne Calder shares more ways to help students improve their thinking.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Teaching students to fact-check what they “think they know” helps them update false beliefs.
  • Students can learn that changing their minds in response to better evidence is a sign of good judgment.
  • Decision-making routines strengthen critical thinking, communication, and respectful disagreement.
Source: Saung Digital/Unsplash, used with permission

Part 2 in a Two-Part Series.

In Part 1 of this interview, I introduced Joanne Calder, an Alliance Senior Teaching Fellow with the Alliance for Decision Education, teaching middle school-aged students in British Columbia. For more than 20 years, Calder has researched critical thinking skills and has turned her findings into fun, effective teaching strategies that help students question, discuss, and update their thinking. This is a continuation of our discussion:

JR: What are other strategies you use to help students keep their thinking flexible and evidence-based?

JC: A fantastic activity I use regularly came from decision scientist Lee Failing: “Endorse, accept, oppose.” I use this when making class decisions such as, “How should we arrange our desks?” I have students stand on a continuum across the classroom based on their opinion. One side of the room represents “endorse” and the other side “oppose.” Everything in between represents “accept.”

Source: Joanne Calder, used with permission

For example, if after identifying what is important to us about our desk arrangement and generating options, we seem to be leaning toward sitting in partnered rows, I will have students stand in the space that reflects their viewpoint on that option. If they love that choice, they stand in “endorse.” If they can’t live with that choice, they stand in “oppose.” If they are somewhere in the middle, they stand along the “accept” continuum, in the spot that most reflects their opinion.

Source: Joanne Calder, used with permission

I then ask students why they are standing where they are standing. If some students are in “opposed,” we ask what we need to do to have them “endorse” or “accept” this choice. For example, one year, students standing in “opposed” agreed to move to “accept” if they could sit with a friend on the first seating plan (we move monthly), and another time students in “opposed” preferred a group seating arrangement; the rest of us agreed to move to a group arrangement every third month.

article continues after advertisement

I also use this exercise for current events: “What do you think of the plan to build a new bridge?” “Schools should have a dress code.” “Solar panels would be a good alternative energy source for our community.” Students need to give a reason for why they chose to stand where they have, and they are encouraged to shift their stance if they hear a compelling reason from another student.

JR: What are strategies that help students consider others' perspectives?

JC: I love community-based inquiry projects. One of the best ones we’ve done was on how our community could be more accessible. We walked all over town with clipboards analyzing our built environment and talking to and interviewing all kinds of people, from grandparents to city policymakers. We considered many different points of view when deciding on our recommendations and advocating for change.

Another way to have students consider differing perspectives is through literature. I find that stories are often safe for students to engage in values and identity work, since the characters in books have a degree of separation. Developing identity and a strong sense of self is important when making decisions so students know what they value when choosing objectives.

I have a series of thinking prompts and sentence starters related to core values, perspectives, and decision-making that students use for literature circles. Recently, one group of students in a literature circle discussion identified what they thought the core values were of three different characters and, as a result, decided which of those characters would make the best friend.

item.title: Do You Struggle With Making Decisions and Choice Overload?
item.description:
Decision-Making

Do You Struggle With Making Decisions and Choice Overload?

New research on the benefits of having fewer choices in day-to-day life.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Life is filled with all kinds of choices.
  • People are more likely to take action when there are fewer choices.
  • It can be helpful to limit your time and energy for selection or choose from fewer options.
Source: Key Therapeutic Art / Pixabay

Sometimes it’s hard to make decisions. How many different choices did you make at the grocery store or while shopping online? How did you choose to spend any unscheduled time last week? What kind of electronic devices do you choose to use?

Today’s world is filled with a multitude of choices about a myriad of things. And life’s choices invite us to a variety of emotions and possibilities, a range of actions and inactions.

From styles of clothing and shoes, to where we search on the internet or social media, to choices about what we eat, how we exercise, and what podcasts or cable shows we consume, choices abound.

It may seem like having loads of choices is all positive, but research indicates that this is not the case. According to Harvard Health (2026), more options also present more possibilities for worry and regret.

A recent study of student engagement in climate-friendly behaviors found that participants with more limited choices selected a greater proportion of actions than students who had more extensive choices did (Bui et al., 2025).

Research by Iyengar and Lepper (2000) found that people were more likely to take action when they had six choices rather than 24. These results challenge the common idea that more choices are better. The study found that people were more likely to buy chocolates or gourmet jams or to do optional class essay assignments when they had only six choices rather than 24 or 30 options.

Psychologist Barry Schwartz, Ph.D., explains that we must make decisions repeatedly throughout our lives, and these choices, big and small, have left us not more liberated but more stuck, not happier but more dissatisfied (2007). In other words, having lots of choices can feel like being stuck in the mud, leading to paralysis rather than freedom. And sometimes the effect of an abundance of choices can be not making any choice at all.

How can you lessen the negative impact of an overload of choices?

Harvard Health (2026) suggests that if your decision is a minor one, it may be helpful to limit the time and energy devoted to the selection or to choose from fewer options. Then, after you make the decision, try to avoid second-guessing your choice.

It can be helpful to be aware of your expectations—to ask yourself whether they are realistic. Is the effort needed to make a “perfect” decision worth the time and effort it will require? For some choices, the answer may be yes. Yet for less significant choices, lowering your expectations and learning to accept a good-enough decision may be helpful.

item.title: The Freddy Krueger Technique of Purging Intrusive Thoughts
item.description:
OCD

The Freddy Krueger Technique of Purging Intrusive Thoughts

How to disempower unwanted scary thoughts by confronting them in imagination.

Posted September 2, 2026

In psychotherapy, bibliotherapy can be useful. But can a theme from a horror film be good therapy? A central idea from the Nightmare on Elm Street flicks can ground a technique in psychotherapy that I have found useful in working with clients with intrusive thoughts.

In one case, a client was referred to me with “pure O,” a type of obsessive-compulsive disorder that is not manifested in compulsive behavior but rather purely obsessive thoughts. This client worked as a limo driver and had the intrusive thought of his right foot becoming paralyzed when driving a passenger to their destination. The thought of the thought led the client to take time off from his job; he contemplated a different line of work to avoid the thought. However, the thought began to emerge while driving and not on the job.

My approach uses logic-based therapy (LBT), a form of rational-emotive behavior therapy I created that utilizes philosophy and logic to help clients overcome self-destructive emotions. One technique I use with clients suffering intrusive thoughts is philosophical imagery, in which the client first imagines themselves being back in a previous situation in which a thought intruded into their mind space. The client then assesses how bad the thought feels by using a negativity scale of 0 to 10, where 10 is the worst and 0 is neutral. Next, the client examines the thought while imagining it, contemplating a resonant philosophical mantra, combined with mindful breathing and supportive imagery. The client then rates the thought on the same scale while in this state of mindful breathing and contemplation.

In LBT, every flawed or irrational way we speak has a specific positive character trait or virtue that can fix it. Catastrophizing is matched to courage. This means identifying a philosophy that builds courage from the client’s perspective and overcomes the tendency to catastrophize. This is because courage is itself a philosophical construct that takes on different meanings for different clients depending on their worldview. In LBT, the client’s worldview is assessed, and the client chooses a mantra that builds the virtue in question from a worldview orientation. Worldviews can be existential, humanistic, theistic, ethical, pragmatic, mindfulness-based, and or stoic. This client tended to be existential. That is, the client felt empowered by contemplating freedom and autonomy over their own thoughts, feelings, and actions.

LBT provides a Toolbox of potentially client-resonant “philosophical antidotes” categorized by the specific virtue and worldview. For example, a client can search the courage category from each of the aforementioned worldview perspectives and receive a list of antidotes that can build courage from the selected worldview. Accordingly, I instructed my client to find a philosophical antidote or mantra for courage from the existential category that resonated with him—a mantra that felt compelling and empowering. The client selected the following antidote:

  • Antidote: "The only way to deal with fear is to face it directly."—Source: Søren Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety
  • Category: Existential Antidote
  • Appeal:
    • Resilience and Growth Appeal: Frames fear as a challenge to overcome rather than avoid.
    • Heroic and Aspirational Appeal: Encourages individuals to rise above fear by confronting it courageously.
  • Analysis: Courage is built through direct engagement with fear, leading to personal growth and empowerment.
  • Language Sensitivity: Replace “I can’t face this” with “I grow stronger by confronting my fears.”
  • Actionable Component: Identify one fear you’ve been avoiding. Take one small, direct action to address it today.
article continues after advertisement

During the next session, I asked the client to imagine that they were driving a passenger and the thought of their right foot becoming paralyzed intruded into their mind space. When the client confirmed that the thought was in mind, I asked them to rate how it felt. They gave the thought a 10 on the 10-point negativity scale.

I then asked the client to think, "The only way to deal with fear is to face it directly. This will make me stronger.” I instructed him to breathe in the strength of facing fear directly (through the nose) and breathe out (through the mouth) the intruding thought, using imagery such as the exhaled thought dropping into a box with a lid closing on it. This client used imagery of the thought evaporating into the clouds when exhaled.

The client proceeded with the exercise while I observed him for about a minute until his breathing appeared more relaxed. I then asked him to rate the idea again, while he continued to contemplate the mantra. The client now gave the thought a 0 on the same negativity scale.

Like the Nightmare on Elm Street character, Freddy Krueger, the thought only had power over the client when he feared it. When the client confronted the thought directly in his imagination and drew strength from it, the thought no longer had power over the client. It was nothing, a goose egg on the negativity scale.

On the other hand, this client had previously tried distraction as a way of dealing with the thought, for example, trying to engage in talking to his customers while driving, but the thought kept re-emerging when the client stopped distracting himself. This is because distraction dignified the thought as something substantial or real, something to try to escape.

What if these thoughts have no existential merit? Why try to escape a thought with no referent? Why run from literally nothing?

There is a logical error known as the reification fallacy: supposing that because we can imagine or speak about something that it must exist. It's like saying that because we can imagine Freddy (or a unicorn), then such a thing exists. However, statements about non-existent objects are false, not true. They make existential claims (something corresponds to a given description) that are simply false.

By facing the thought directly, the client no longer had to hide from it, and the thought ceased to exercise power over him. Like Freddy, the thought had no ontological status of its own. It was just an empty vessel, an image of a false description in the client’s fearful imagination, just like Freddy in the dreams of those who feared him. When the client looked the fear in the face, there was literally nothing to fear.

item.title: When Being Great at Your Job Isn’t Enough for Leadership
item.description:
Leadership

When Being Great at Your Job Isn’t Enough for Leadership

Exploring the inner work of making the shift from expert to leader

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Technical excellence builds careers, but senior impact depends on presence, relationships, and influence.
  • If visibility feels like self-promotion, tactics won't stick—inner work has to prepare the terrain first.
  • Leader stereotypes skew masculine, and self-promotion can risk backlash.
  • Hesitation is normal, but it caps careers.
Source: Henrimeilhac / Unsplash

Over the years, I have coached many accomplished women who built impressive careers on technical excellence. Then, at the senior level, they hit a wall they never saw coming: the excellence that got them here stops moving them forward.

Their work is strong, but they’re not necessarily seen as leaders. They’re respected but don’t have the influence they need to advance their work and careers. They’re in the room, but may not be shaping the conversation. And they’re genuinely puzzled—because they’re doing everything right, and it’s no longer enough.

The Expert-to-Leader Shift

At senior levels, impact depends less on what you personally deliver and more on how you show up, the relationships you build, and your ability to influence others.

This is the expert-to-leader transition, and it demands both inner and outer work.

The inner work is about examining and strengthening your relationship to your confidence, strengths, values, status, and personal power. It influences how women show up and see themselves as leaders, and creates the space for the outer work. The outer work provides the skills required to lead.

In my coaching experience, without the inner work, the skills rarely take hold. Making your work and your team’s work understood and valued, building relationships that generate insight, perspective, and opportunity, and gathering intelligence to understand how decisions get made—these are precisely the activities many women dislike most.

Why Tactical Advice Can Fall Flat

The standard response is tactical: speak up more, build your network, promote your accomplishments.

The advice is not wrong—it just tends not to take root.

If visibility feels like self-promotion, you will find reasons to avoid it. If networking feels inauthentic, you will let invitations slide. If naming your accomplishments feels like bragging, you will deflect credit and stay invisible. No amount of strategy survives contact with a belief system that says, “This is not who I am.”

This is why leadership development for women so often fails to stick: it hands women tactics to adopt without preparing the terrain in which those tactics can grow in.

Why This Is Harder for Women

This is not every woman’s experience—plenty never hit this wall. But for those who do, the problem is real and has identifiable roots.

article continues after advertisement

Research shows that our mental image of “a leader” still skews masculine. When the prototype does not look like you, it is harder to see yourself in the role—and harder for others to see you there.

Leadership identity is not something you simply decide to have. It develops through a social process of claiming and granting: you build a leader identity through claiming—the leadership actions you take—and others grant it, or do not, through their responses. For women, the cycle is more fragile: claims are granted less readily, feedback is more ambiguous, and each ungranted claim makes the next one feel riskier.

Add the backlash effect—women who self-promote are judged more capable but less likable and penalized for it—and resisting visibility looks less like a confidence problem and more like an accurate reading of a real bind. The hesitation is not irrational, but left unexamined, it quietly caps a career.

What Inner Work Actually Means

Inner work is not therapy or affirmations. It is the deliberate practice of building a leadership identity robust enough to see yourself as a leader and make room for the outer work.

It involves five practices:

Managing self-doubt. Not eliminating it. Rather, developing a practice for handling the narratives that ask, “Who are you to think you can lead this project?” or “What makes you think you’re ready for the bigger role?” as part of taking action and building leadership experiences and confidence.

Owning your accomplishments. Many women I coach struggle to articulate what they have achieved and become even more uncomfortable when they need to talk about it. The work is building an accurate account of your contribution, finding language to own it, and managing the discomfort to say it.

Taking values-based action. Some necessary leadership skills and behaviors can feel unpalatable. However, when approached through your values—advancing your ideas, your work, and your team, or leveraging relationships to advance a program of work—they are done differently, and they feel different.

Exercising your status and personal power. According to Alison Fragale, your status is the extent to which you are valued, admired, and respected—and intentionally managing how you demonstrate warmth and competence is a pathway to building status. Similarly, acting with agency and cultivating boundaries is a way to demonstrate personal power.

article continues after advertisement

Wearing your leadership identity. Moving from “I’m a technical expert who sometimes leads” to “I’m a leader who brings deep expertise” is the key shift. Expertise does not disappear. It becomes the platform rather than the identity, creating space for a leadership identity to emerge, become internalized, and be communicated outwardly.

The Terrain Changes Everything

In my experience, when we start with the inner work, the outer work stops feeling like a betrayal of self and starts feeling like an expression of it. Networking can be reimagined as gathering perspective and building genuine relationships. Visibility can become a way to ensure your team’s work lands where it matters. Navigating organizational dynamics can be reframed as stewardship—ensuring good work and good people get seen.

The benefits extend beyond the individual woman: her team gains an advocate, and her organization gains a leader who can move ideas, not just execute them.

So the reflection I will leave you with is this: If being great at your job is no longer enough, what shift in how you see yourself might make the difference?

Tactics can be learned in a workshop. An identity is built deliberately, over time. Being great at your job got you here. Leading beyond it starts with wearing your leadership.

item.title: The 10 Minutes After Your Child Loses It Matter Most
item.description:
Parenting

The 10 Minutes After Your Child Loses It Matter Most

What parents do immediately after a blow up can restart the conflict or calm it.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • The first 10 minutes after a blow up is crucial.
  • The aftermath of a blowup is often more crucial than doling out consequences.
  • A brief period of calm, followed by a low-pressure reconnection helps change the pattern.

As parents, we have all been there when a child yells, storms upstairs, and slams the door. When parents and kids unpack these tense situations in my office, I hear all the details of these heated conflicts. Eventually, we get to the part of the story where the house goes quiet again. That is, in many ways, where the emotion dysregulation part of the story truly stops, or maybe that is right before round two starts. For many parents, that blissful quiet period feels like a nice opening. They think, usually erroneously, "Now is when we should deal with what just happened, before it gets forgotten."

Following Your Child Upstairs Creates More Chaos

Parents want to get their point across, but you may want to check out a recent post of mine about those cherished "teachable moments" that keep failing. The parent follows the child or teen (or even adult child), catches up, and says things like: "We need to talk about your behavior." Or, "You cannot speak to me that way." Or, one of my favorites that cooks up even more chaos: "Come back downstairs now and apologize!" All these reactions are understandable. Yet the problem is that the child's nervous system has only started to settle down. What looks like that prized teachable moment often slips into round two of the conflict.

You've Heard Timing Matters, It Really Does

A calmer response to the above scenarios might be, "We are both upset about this right now. Let's talk about this later." That is what I mean by calm, firm, and noncontrolling, as I further explain in my new book: 24 Hours to a Less Defiant Child. Calm does not mean permissive, and firm doesn't mean harsh, and noncontrolling does not mean abdicating your authority. Can you see that this means resisting the urge to force insight, cooperation, or even an apology, for that matter, when your child is emotionally not able to give you any of those? The calm, firm, non-controlling approach will work far better than a lecture through the closed bedroom door featuring a 10-minute explanation of why the child's behavior was unacceptable.

Your Takeaway: Changing a Difficult Parent-Child Pattern Can Be Much Easier

Changing a challenging parent-child dynamic usually doesn't require a parenting overhaul. Sometimes it all begins with how you handle one crucial moment. The next time the door slams and the house goes quiet, it may be best for you, as a parent, to zip it, lock it, and put it in your pocket. Yes, you may be worried about your child "getting away with it." Yet waiting until your child (at any age) can actually hear you in a calm, constructive conversation may make the accountability you want far more likely.

item.title: The Relationship Isn't Right for You, but Why Do You Stay?
item.description:
Relationships

The Relationship Isn't Right for You, but Why Do You Stay?

Early family dynamics may shape what we accept as normal love.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us have stayed in unhealthy or even abusive relationships, long past their expiration date.
  • Early family experiences may impact your expectations of adult relationships.
  • Developing self-awareness and self-compassion can help reverse these patterns.

Ivan was in his second marriage, again with a woman who was unkind to him and who made him feel bad about himself. We had been exploring this in therapy, as he had expressed interest in wanting to end the relationship, but felt overcome with anxiety at the thought of being alone.

The relationships Ivan was exposed to in childhood taught him the template for the relationships he would come to expect in adulthood. He learned that relationships were abusive, that people would be manipulative and unkind, and that they were unreliable. He learned that people would be unkind.

Source: Image by Hasan Mazloom from Pixabay

Early family experiences may affect your expectations of adult relationships

Many of us who were taught in childhood that we were unlovable and difficult go on to expect these things in the relationships around us. We may develop an anxious attachment where we cling to any semblance of connection or love, anything that will tell our inner child and self-blaming brain that we are worthy of love. Others may push away from relationships altogether, scared of repeating the same patterns that left them feeling alone and shamed.

I can relate to this. Throughout my adult life, I have explored, with therapy and self-reflection, how the relationships I was exposed to in childhood taught me the template for the relationships I would come to expect in adulthood. I learned that relationships were abusive, that people would be manipulative and unkind, and that they were unreliable. I learned that people would be unkind. I expected this because it was what I knew. Now I help clients like Ivan understand these same patterns and work to unlearn them.

This is an important part of understanding why we sometimes stay in relationships that, from the outside, seem so obviously wrong for us. We aren't always choosing what is healthy. Sometimes, we are choosing what is familiar. And when what is familiar is dysfunction, or someone who makes us feel bad about ourselves, it can take work to recognize that something being familiar doesn't mean it is what we deserve.

Maybe we developed an anxious attachment where we cling to any small sign of connection or love, anything that will tell our inner child and self-blaming brain that we are worthy of love. Others may push away from relationships altogether, scared to repeat the same patterns that left them feeling alone and shamed.

Developing self-awareness and self-compassion can help reverse these patterns

Know that things can change. It takes time, self-reflection, and a journey of going inward. For Ivan, and others like him, it meant looking honestly at the relationships he had chosen, the things he had tolerated, and the reasons he had been so desperate to feel loved and wanted. It meant understanding why he had stayed, and that understanding his reasons does not mean he had to repeat the pattern.

article continues after advertisement

You can learn that you are worthy of love and deserve to be treated with respect and validation. You can learn to recognize the difference between someone liking you and someone being a good, healthy fit for you.

And you don't have to settle.
