item.title: Practical Parenting Tools for Traumatized Children
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Practical Parenting Tools for Traumatized Children

Adoptive and foster parenting skills can benefit all parents and professionals.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Love is usually not enough for traumatized adopted and foster children.
  • Caregivers need additional practical tools to support, correct, and guide these children.
  • These tools must be applied repeatedly, kindly, calmly, and firmly to help the children heal.
  • These tools can benefit all parents and health professionals.

This post is part of a series on adverse childhood experiences. Read the other parts here.

Many adoptive and foster parents earnestly believe that love will heal their children’s traumatic wounds, only to encounter unexpected challenges that they’re ill-prepared to handle. Overwhelming childhood upheaval, including separation from biological parents, neglect, abuse, and other trauma and attachment disruptions, impairs normal brain development. What looks like defiance and retreating from affection really reflects damaged brain wiring and learned distrust, fear, and survival strategies.

In The Connected Parent, renowned child development expert, parent, and foster parent Dr. Karyn Purvis and co-author Lisa Qualls offer practical parenting skills for children with a hard start—skills that all parents and health professionals will find useful. Purvis optimistically notes: “I’ve never yet seen a child who couldn’t experience dramatic levels of healing. The greatest predictor of a child’s capacity for healing is a safe, nurturing adult who can help them learn to trust.”

To help their brains heal, “children from hard places” need parents whose love and dedication are matched by special skills (many common parenting strategies are actually counterproductive for traumatized children);

  • Physical support to promote the rewiring of impaired brain circuitry. Good nutrition, regular snacks every few hours, hydration, enjoyable exercise, the right kinds and amount of sensory stimulation, and regular sleep are all critical.
  • Emotional support: Countless acts that say, “I’m here, I care for you no matter what, you can trust me” gradually begin to replace the learned perspective that adults can’t be trusted and that they’re no good. Parents who stop and give full presence to children when they talk, eyes meeting, begin to meet the unmet attachment needs of these children.
  • Correction, especially when the child is calm and alert, and physical needs are met. Respectful communication is consistently modeled and taught to the child.
  • Parents who have settled their own traumatic wounds so that they can model a pathway to healing for their children. Instead of being triggered by a child’s disrespect, healed parents can breathe through their children’s disrespect and respond effectively.

Real-life skills

1. Connect, then correct. If the child disrespectfully demands a drink, get down to their eye level. Calmly and warmly say, “Look right here. Let me see your beautiful eyes. I love your eyes. Good job showing your eyes. I’m listening, and I want to help you, but you need to ask respectfully. Let’s try that again with respect.”

2. Share your power. When possible, give the child two choices to feel a measure of control (that they probably lacked earlier). “I see that you weren’t able to play nicely with your sister. Would you like to sit at the counter and draw or rock with me?”

3. Compromise. If a child balks at the two choices given by the parent, the parent might say, “It sounds like you’re asking for a compromise. Could you use your good words and ask me with respect?” The child might ask, “Could I play some more before I go to bed?” The mother responds, “Let’s set a timer for five more minutes, and when the timer goes off, you go to bed. My end of the bargain is I let you play; your end of the bargain is when the timer goes off, it’s time for bed. A deal?”

article continues after advertisement

4. Nurture as often as possible. One-on-one time builds trust and meets unmet attachment needs: do chores, run errands, have VIP nights or cook together, help with homework, and have bedtime routines and stories. If children have nightmares, they can sleep in a sleeping bag or a play tent beside the parents’ bed. Take walks together, playfully feed each other popcorn if they allow it, sing songs, place notes in lunch bags. With full presence, listen without interrupting. Reassure them that you care (“I’ll always listen, but please use respect”). Rather than sending them to their room if defiant, which increases a sense of isolation, bring them close. Have them sit in a thinking spot nearby when misbehaving until they are calmer and ready to talk.

Recently, a father’s seven-year-old threw a tantrum and wouldn’t follow the rules of a game. The father, without anger, carried her to the car and said, “I love you and want to help you learn how to act. Sit here until you are ready to talk. I’ll be right here.” A few minutes later, after their talk, she was smiling and playing nicely with the other children. At times, you might even try returning to the original spot to act out the better way.

5. Regulate yourself (take a breath), then regulate the child. The parent says warmly, “I can see this is hard for you, and I want to help. Let’s see if we can figure this out.” If the child is highly agitated, use as few words as possible, since a brain on high alert can’t handle too many words (“Whoa, show respect.”). If a child is too loud, you might calmly say, “Match my voice.”

6. Playfully practice right and wrong behaviors. Mother: “When I say, ‘Please come to dinner,’ what would be the wrong way to act?” After the child dramatically acts out the wrong way, going ballistic, the mother says, “Good job practicing no respect. Now, let’s try again with respect.” The mother says, “Dear, it’s time to come to dinner.” The child says, “Okay, Mom,” and the mother says, “Great job. High five.”

7. Validate and calm strong emotions. “Dear, you look angry, but I can see your heart is actually feeling sad. It’s okay to let go of mad and feel sad. Can you use your words and tell me what you feel? Or would you like to draw what you are feeling?”

Purvis and Qualls explain many other helpful parenting strategies, including how to adapt the above skills to teens. Adoptive and foster parents need to remember that traumatized children need repeated application of tools like these to build trust and rewire maladaptive neural pathways imprinted by mistreatment. Be patient and kind with yourself as you navigate the difficult challenges. No one does this perfectly.

item.title: Destroy the Stormtrooper: On the Perils of Dehumanization
item.description:
Media

Destroy the Stormtrooper: On the Perils of Dehumanization

Star Wars villains shed light on the human capacity to make monsters of others.

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Star Wars Stormtroopers are designed to blur human and monstrous, making violence against them feel justified.
  • Fictional dehumanization feels safe, but in reality, it undermines empathy and enables real harm.
  • Recognizing the mental process of dehumanization can help us resist making “monsters” of others.

Consider, for a moment, the Stormtroopers in the movie Star Wars. We like to joke about how they cannot seem to fire their guns accurately or how they are simple-minded. But there is also something very unnerving about them. They are humans, but at the same time, they are also monstrous. They have arms, legs, a head, and a torso, just like the rest of us. But they are completely armored, with no skin showing. They wear a mask that resembles a skull, and they speak as if through a robotic filter. They are, to put it one way, uncanny.

In a famous essay on the uncanny, Freud asserted that there is great fear to be had in things that look human but are not-quite-human, such as wax figures. The wax figure resembles a person, but it is not. It might seem amusing at first, but also unnerving. Similarly, the Stormtrooper walks and talks like a human, but it is also so armored and robotic that it becomes uncanny. And, of course, the Stormtrooper is out for blood.

In the original Star Wars, Stormtroopers are bent on destroying the heroic rebels at all costs. Their role seems to be firing indiscriminately at the good guys. The good guys, in turn, blast away at the Stormtroopers, felling them by the score. The audience cheers as Han Solo, Luke Skywalker, and Princess Leia mow down the skull-visaged baddies. At one point, aboard the Death Star, Luke and Han go undercover, donning the Stormtrooper uniform themselves. However, the audience knows they are not bad—they soon take off the helmets to show us that we can cheer them on as they destroy more nameless Stormtroopers.

One reason why it is so easy to cheer on the rebels is that the Stormtroopers are human, but also not-human. That is, while we do recognize there are people inside those suits, the suits themselves communicate a demonic presence, which makes mowing them down less troubling than it might be if they were dressed in more revealing clothes. They are, to use an apt term, monstrous.

In the book Making Monsters: The Uncanny Power of Dehumanization, philosopher David Livingstone Smith makes a very interesting and provocative argument: when we demonize the enemy, we see them as both subhuman monsters and as complete human beings. This, he recognizes, is illogical. You cannot be both human and non-human, right? But here’s his point: our brains do not always travel along logical lines. We are capable of believing contradictory things simultaneously when and if it serves our purposes.

Here’s an example that Smith gives: The Nazis depicted Jews as both “rats” and “criminals.” Rats are animals, and thus not human beings. Criminals, on the other hand, are human beings. Smith notes that this contradiction is essential to understanding the act of dehumanization: “there is an important research literature… that suggests that contradictory beings like rat/ ­humans elicit a distinctive and highly disturbing psychological response. They are felt to be what in German is called Unheimlich, a word that is conventionally (if imperfectly) translated as ‘uncanny.’”

article continues after advertisement

Uncanny monsters, other theorists tell us, are frightening because they don’t fit into our socially ascribed categories. But they are close enough to being human that we become disoriented by them. The abominable snowman, for example, walks about like a person, but it is covered in fur and has supernatural strength. A zombie looks like a person, but it has rotting skin and a mindless craving for brains. The Creature from the Black Lagoon is humanoid and can live on land, but it can also breathe underwater and has green skin, gills, and a creepy face. In other words, such monsters are uncanny—human-but-not-human. This makes them disorienting and frightening. Exactly like Stormtroopers.

A study of dehumanization by two psychologists found that a key part of dehumanization is failing to take the “mind” of the dehumanized into account. If the dehumanized person’s mind is not considered valid, then that person may not be treated as if they exist within the same moral framework as the victimizer. The researchers summarize: “Dehumanized perception of extreme outgroups suggests that they are perceived as unlike all other people. Thus, discriminatory or inhumane behaviors may not seem to matter because one fails to consider the person’s mental experience. Having a mind is a uniquely human trait, suggesting dehumanized others may be treated more like objects in the environment without internal states.” The result of such thinking can often lead to horrendous acts of violence against the “non-humans.”

To dehumanize, in sum, seems to be a common human act. Our minds are flexible, and when helped along by fear, we can see people as both containing personhood and as being alien to personhood. When this happens, we are more likely to treat the “monster” of this process “more like objects” than people. We undermine our natural empathy and find a target of wrath instead. We justify committing violence against them.

It is worth recognizing the mental processes behind dehumanization. In fiction, it is harmless and can help audiences cheer on good guys battling robotic space thugs. In the real world, though, it is important to see the process of dehumanization at work. We should never create “monsters” out of real, living people.

item.title: Can a Blood Test Predict Your Risk of Alzheimer’s Disease?
item.description:
Dementia

Can a Blood Test Predict Your Risk of Alzheimer’s Disease?

Should you ask your doctor to check your amyloid levels?

Posted September 2, 2026

Key points
  • Blood tests approved by the FDA in 2025 are promising to look at amyloid and tau levels via blood samples.
  • These proteins are present in blood at much weaker levels than in brain tissue.
  • The results may determine one's risk for AD, exclude AD, or, in the presence of symptoms, confirm a diagnosis.
  • Discussing any cognitive changes with your doctor is important; testing is one part of a wider conversation.

Going to the doctor to have tests done has become part of our everyday lives. Often, these checks are done because of symptoms you have experienced, and the doctor is looking to rule in or rule out the possibility that particular causes are behind how you are feeling. But sometimes blood tests can be used as a means of risk assessment. Rather than telling the clinician and patient whodunnit, they merely suggest which way around the board you’d benefit from moving to.

Historically, Alzheimer’s disease was only diagnosed postmortem

When a patient’s brain was dissected, a series of consistent changes found within brain cells and surrounding tissues confirmed that they had indeed had Alzheimer’s disease. Key to these findings was the visibility of excessive amyloid plaques—a specific type of protein—between brain cells. Alongside this finding was that of tau, another protein, that caused tangles within these brain cells. This, combined with inflammation, increased brain cell shrinkage, and premature death, is a key finding in the brains of those with Alzheimer’s disease.

Scientists knew they had to find a way to see this buildup of excessive amyloid earlier to aid diagnosis and ultimately treatment

Testing and diagnosis evolved for both imaging—in the form of PET scans, a type of MRI scan that uses a radioactive tracer to confirm or rule out the presence of amyloid and tau proteins—and biology. A lumbar puncture could be done to take a sample of spinal fluid, which could be looked at under a microscope for these two proteins. For the last few years, this has become the gold standard for making a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease.

But problems remain in real life—the reluctance of patients to attend an assessment for fear of this condition, then the long delays in assessment at specialist services, combined with a lack of access to these expensive scanners and/or accessibility for lumbar puncture tests. Researchers have known this for decades. Clinicians and patients have done the best they can with the tools at their disposal. The results often include delays in diagnosis, a clinical picture indicating diagnosis in the absence of pathology, and a ticking time bomb of overwhelmed patients and carers trying to do their best for their loved ones with minimal resources.

This might be all about to change

Blood tests approved by the FDA in 2025 are promising to look at amyloid and tau levels via simple blood samples. The results may determine either your risk for developing AD or, if in the presence of symptoms, whether you actually already have it.

Here’s what we know:

article continues after advertisement

May 2025: Lumipulse G pTau217/Beta-Amyloid Ratio (Fujirebio)

Lumipulse G was approved by the FDA for use in symptomatic adults aged 55 and older. This looks at both amyloid and tau, and the ratio between these two levels. Why? P Tau increases when there is a buildup of a specific form of amyloid. The amyloid level itself, however, appears to go down—the idea being that the amyloid gets stuck inside the cells.

This test made headlines as it looked at both key markers, but also because the blood results matched the findings from PET and CSF tests and at very high levels. Specifically, it had a Positive Predictive Value (PPV) of 97.1 percent against the gold standard results from a group of patients seen in a memory clinic.

October 2025: Elecsys pTau181 (Roche)

As well as looking at only one biomarker, this targets a different population. This is designed for use in primary care, and the idea is it’s a rule-out test. So if you have symptoms that raise the alarm for cognitive changes, but this test confirms your pTau 181 level is normal, you can be reassured Alzheimer’s disease is not the cause at the time of the test.

August 2026

Two more tests have been cleared: PrecivityAD2 (C2N Diagnostics) was first cleared down to age 40 but still requires symptoms and clinical evaluation. Elecsys pTau217 (Roche/Eli Lilly) is the newest single-biomarker test for those over 55 who have symptoms or complaints of cognitive decline.

I’m worried I’ve got Alzheimer’s: Should I be asking my doctor for one of these tests?

I think the first thing to emphasize is that these tests represent a huge scientific leap forward. Incredible progress has been made in the worlds of research and pharma, which have combined to create blood testing options that will make an impactful change in people’s lives. However, the data is not yet available to confirm how these tests impact quality of life or the progression of disease. But it can’t be, because the tests have just been approved.

article continues after advertisement

For patients, this can feel confusing. These proteins are present in blood at much weaker levels than in brain tissue, so the science required to reliably detect them in the right people at the right time has a big job to do. Only time and more data, both from people and lab-based, will really determine which tests provide the most accurate benefit for those who need them most. Discussing any cognitive changes with your doctor is important, and looking at testing is just one part of that wide conversation.

Things to be aware of

  • The test with the most accurate data so far is the Lumipulse—this was a sample from patients in a memory clinic vs. primary care, with a higher prevalence of amyloid already, which may impact the positive predictive value. It was also in a population that was 84 percent white, so demographic data is still to come.

  • Abnormal kidney function due to kidney disease or some medications can skew these results, so it’s important to be aware of this, too.

  • Is there a conflict of interest? The labs behind the development of these tests are also part of the companies that are trialing medications to reduce amyloid levels in the brain. This is not unusual, but it’s something to be remembered when reading reports in the media.

  • A positive test result doesn’t confirm AD in the absence of symptoms. All the tests that have been approved state this implicitly, and the results need to be interpreted with caution by a trained clinician who understands these findings and the clinical picture the patient presents with.

Will testing for amyloid eventually be like having a cholesterol check with your primary care doctor?

The idea behind this statement is a good one—accessible testing, stigma reduction, and a biomarker that is routinely measured and tracked over time to evaluate disease risk. This will also generate more data to inform research trials and, in time, treatment for patients. But this may be putting the cart before the horse—we are a long way from being set up for this in primary care, and there is still a very different psychological impact of being told you have something that might increase your chance of having a neurodegenerative condition, for which there remains no accessible risk free cure, versus using lifestyle changes and statins if appropriate to reduce your cholesterol.

article continues after advertisement

But will these tests help us get closer to testing for AD in everyday life? Only time, and more research, will tell.
